659.title: The gold-washer
659.hook: gold refined from coarse to fine impurities, step by step (AN 3, the gold-washer)
659.howItsDone: Buddhist training in many traditions is taught as gradual, beginning with ethical conduct and moving to meditation and wisdom, and teachers often use the gold-washer to describe that order.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of the Kalama talk, and your line, one kind act, one clean choice. Today the Book of Threes takes us to a riverbank, where a man is washing dirt for gold.

Cleaning out a garage has an order. First the big stuff: the broken bike, the boxes of who knows what. Then the medium stuff: tools, cans, things to sort. Then the fine stuff: dust, cobwebs, the last screws in the corner. Nobody starts with the cobwebs while the bike's still in the way. The Buddha used a picture like that, from a trade his listeners could watch at work: someone standing in a river, washing gravel to find gold.
screen: `CLEANING OUT A GARAGE.` → `BIG STUFF FIRST, THEN DUST.` → `A MAN WASHING GRAVEL FOR GOLD.`

segments.voice: Raw gold, the Buddha says, has coarse impurities: soil, sand, grit and gravel. The gold-washer pours it into a trough and rinses them away. Then the medium ones, fine grit and coarse sand. Then the fine ones, fine sand and black dust. What's left is gold dust. The goldsmith puts it in a crucible and blows on it, again and again. At first it isn't workable; it hasn't let go of all its dross. At last it becomes soft, pliable and bright, ready for any ornament he wants: a ring, earrings, a chain. Then the Buddha maps it onto a person in training. The coarse impurities are misconduct of body, speech and mind. Those go first. The medium ones are thoughts of sensual desire, ill will and harming. The fine ones: thoughts about one's family, one's home country, one's reputation. Then even thoughts about the teaching itself, a kind of busy spiritual chatter, are let go. And the mind becomes steady, unified and workable, like the gold. It's an honest picture of change. The order is practical: you don't work on subtle thoughts while you're still lying to people. And the pace is slow. Each stage gets its own washing, and even the crucible takes time. The gold doesn't come out bright until it has let go of what isn't gold.
screen: `COARSE, MEDIUM, FINE IMPURITIES` · `GOLD DUST IN THE CRUCIBLE` · `BODY, SPEECH, MIND, THEN THOUGHTS` · `SOFT, BRIGHT, READY TO WORK` · then, large: `REFINED SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Choose one habit you'd like to refine, not remove all at once. Ask, like the gold-washer, what the coarse part is: maybe the action itself, the sharp word, the extra drink, the late night. Picture washing just that layer away, and leave the finer layers, the thoughts and moods underneath, to come in their own time.
The gold-washer. In the Book of Threes, gold is washed of coarse, then medium, then fine impurities, and the mind is refined the same way, step by step. Today's word.
Your line: refined slowly. Nobody expects the whole riverbed to turn to gold in one pass. Day six hundred fifty-nine, done.

660.title: Salt in the river
660.hook: a lump of salt ruins a cup of water but is lost in the Ganges: a broad heart (AN 3, the salt crystal)
660.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the salt simile to explain that karma is not a mechanical tit-for-tat, and many practitioners develop the immeasurables, kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, to widen the heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the gold-washer, and your line, refined slowly. Today, the discourse just before it in the Book of Threes, and a pinch of salt.

Two people tell the same small lie on the same afternoon. One carries it for weeks, and it sours everything around it. The other notices, owns it, and by evening it has barely left a mark. Same lie, same size, very different results. The Buddha takes up a sharper version of that puzzle, about karma. If every act brings back exactly what it deserves, measure for measure, how could anyone ever get free? He answers with something from the kitchen.
screen: `ONE SMALL LIE, TWO PEOPLE.` → `TWO VERY DIFFERENT RESULTS.` → `AN ANSWER FROM THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: He begins by rejecting a claim. If someone says that however a person acts, in exactly that way they'll experience the result, then, he says, there would be no living the holy life, no chance to make a complete end of suffering. Then the picture. Suppose someone drops a lump of salt into a small cup of water. Would the water become salty and undrinkable? Yes, sir, because the cup is small. Now suppose they drop the same lump into the river Ganges. Would the river become undrinkable? No, sir, because the Ganges is a great mass of water. The same small bad deed, he says, can lead one person to great suffering and barely touch another. The difference is in the person. One is undeveloped in body, in conduct, in mind, in wisdom: limited, small-hearted, living with suffering. The other is developed, great-hearted, dwelling in the immeasurable. For them the result of that small act is felt here and now, and not even a trace may appear beyond. He adds a picture almost from a court: one person is jailed for stealing a tiny coin; another, rich and powerful, isn't jailed for the same amount. This isn't a teaching that small harms don't matter. The salt is still salt. It's a teaching that the size of the heart changes what the salt does, and hearts can grow.
screen: `NOT EXACTLY AS YOU ACT, YOU REAP` · `A CUP OF WATER: UNDRINKABLE` · `THE GANGES: STILL CLEAR` · `THE SIZE OF THE HEART` · then, large: `SALT IN THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Recall one small thing that's been bothering you, a comment, a mistake, a slight, and feel how salty it tastes in a small cup. Then let the cup widen: breathe into the chest and imagine the heart as wide as a river, with room for people you love, the sky, this whole day. Place that small salty thing into all of it, and notice whether the taste changes.

661.title: Three intoxications
661.hook: the pride of youth, of health, of life (AN 3.38)
661.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers draw on this discourse when speaking about aging, illness and death, and some meditators reflect on all three as a way to loosen the pride of youth, health and life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a lump of salt and a great river, and your line, widen your heart first. Today the Buddha remembers his own childhood, in his own words.

We've heard the palace story told about him: the sheltered prince, the four sights. In this short discourse from the Book of Threes, the Buddha tells it himself, in startling detail. I was delicate, monks, he says, most delicate. At my father's home, lotus ponds were made just for me, one of blue lotuses, one of red, one of white. I wore only fine cloth from Kasi. A white sunshade was held over me day and night, so cold and heat, dust and dew wouldn't touch me.
screen: `IN HIS OWN WORDS.` → `THREE LOTUS PONDS, BLUE, RED, WHITE.` → `A WHITE SUNSHADE, DAY AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: He had three palaces, one for winter, one for summer, one for the rains. In the rainy months he stayed in the rains palace, entertained by musicians, and didn't come down at all. In other homes, he says, servants were fed broken rice with sour gruel; in his father's house, even the servants ate fine rice and meat. Even with all that, a thought came to me. An untaught person, himself subject to aging, sees someone old and feels disgust and shame, forgetting that he will age too. That isn't fitting for me. As he reflected, the intoxication of youth left him. The same with illness: the untaught are repelled by the sick, though they'll fall ill too, and the intoxication of health left him. The same with death, and the intoxication of life left him. The Pali word is mada, used for drunkenness and for the madness of pride. Youth, health, being alive: none of them are bad. The intoxication is the feeling that they're mine to keep, and that the old, the sick and the dying are some other kind of person. In the very next discourse he names what these three do: a person drunk on youth, health or life acts badly in body, speech and mind. It's easy to see how; the intoxication whispers that there's plenty of time. Not a lecture on aging, then: a man remembering the white sunshade, and the moment he saw it couldn't keep anything off him forever.
screen: `THREE PALACES, ONE FOR EACH SEASON` · `DISGUST AT THE OLD, FORGETTING ONESELF` · `MADA: DRUNK ON YOUTH, HEALTH, LIFE` · `THE SUNSHADE CAN'T KEEP IT OFF` · then, large: `THE THREE INTOXICATIONS.`

segments.voice: Feel the body as it is today, the age it is, the health it has, the life that's in it, and let a little gratitude in for each. Then notice, gently, whether one of the three has a grip of pride: I'm too young for that, I never get sick, there's always tomorrow. Soften it with a plain thought, this too will change, held not with fear but with clearer, kinder eyes toward anyone older or sicker than you.
Three intoxications. In AN 3.38, the Buddha, remembering his sheltered youth, names the pride of youth, of health, and of life, and tells how each one left him. Today's word.
Your line: the three intoxications. Aging, sickness and death are my road too. That's day six hundred sixty-one.

662.title: Remember me as awake
662.hook: Dona asks: are you a god? a spirit? a human? No: awake
662.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell the Dona story to explain the title buddha, 'the awakened one,' and many Buddhists bow to Buddha images as a sign of respect for that awakening rather than as worship of a god.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the three intoxications, the pride of youth, of health and of life. Today a man asks the Buddha what he is, and gets an answer he didn't expect.

A road between two towns. A brahmin named Dona is walking along it, and he stops. In the dust are footprints, and inside each print, the text says, is the mark of a wheel with a thousand spokes, rim and hub complete. These can't be the footprints of a human being, he thinks. So he follows them, off the road, to the foot of a tree, where someone is sitting, calm, senses at rest, mind at peace. Dona walks up and asks a very direct question.
screen: `FOOTPRINTS IN THE DUST.` → `A WHEEL IN EACH ONE.` → `A FIGURE UNDER A TREE.`

segments.voice: It comes in four parts. Will you be a god? No, brahmin. A gandhabba, a heavenly musician? No. A yakkha, a spirit of the forest? No. A human being, then? No, brahmin, I will not be a human being. Dona is baffled: then what will you be? The things that would make him a god, a spirit or a human, the Buddha explains, are the taints, the deep habits of craving and confusion that push a being into one kind of life or another. In him those are abandoned, cut at the root like a palm stump, unable to grow again. Then a picture. A blue or red or white lotus is born in the water, grows up in the water, and rises above it, and the water doesn't cling to it. In the same way, he says, he was born and grew up in the world, but has gone beyond it, and the world doesn't stain him. Then the line: remember me, brahmin, as a buddha. Buddha isn't a name. It's a title: awake, the one who has woken up. Notice what the answer refuses. It won't be filed under any category Dona brought with him. It doesn't claim divinity, and it doesn't settle for being just another person. It points to a state: not asleep. Teachers often use this sutta when someone asks whether Buddhists worship the Buddha as a god. The Buddha's own answer, here, is no.
screen: `A GOD? A SPIRIT? A HUMAN? NO.` · `THE ROOTS ARE CUT.` · `A LOTUS ABOVE THE WATER.` · then, large: `REMEMBER ME AS AWAKE.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest and, for a few breaths, notice whether part of you is half asleep: running a plan, replaying a talk, waiting for the next thing. Then wake up fully to this one moment, the weight of your body, the air on your skin, the sound nearest you. When you drift, that's fine; the drifting is how you learn what waking feels like, so come back and wake again.

Your line: be awake for one moment. Like the lotus, risen clear of the water it grew in. Until tomorrow.

663.title: The firebrand
663.hook: a torch from a funeral pyre is useless; four kinds of people
663.howItsDone: Many Buddhist teachers describe practice as having two sides, working on one's own mind and serving others, and the firebrand sutta is one of the early texts they cite for holding the two together.

segments.voice: Yesterday Dona asked god, spirit or human, and heard a different word: buddha, awake. Your line, be awake for one moment. Today, a piece of burnt wood.

In ancient India the dead were burned on open pyres at the edge of town. When the fire went down, what was left was ash, bone and charred sticks. Picture one of those sticks, burning at both ends and smeared with dung in the middle. Nobody would carry it home for the kitchen fire, or take it into the forest to build with. It's good for nothing, in the village or out of it. The Buddha picks up exactly that stick, in words, and holds it up to a room of monks.
screen: `AFTER THE PYRE.` → `BURNING AT BOTH ENDS.` → `GOOD FOR NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The sutta, in the Book of Fours, sorts people into four kinds. The first practices neither for their own good nor for the good of others. That's the firebrand. The second practices for the good of others, but not their own. The third, for their own good, but not for others. The fourth, for both. Look at the middle two. The Buddha puts the one who works on themselves above the one who works only for others. That can sound selfish, until you see what 'own good' means here: taming greed, hatred and confusion in yourself. Someone who rushes to fix everyone else while their own temper is on fire can make a lot of smoke. The texts elsewhere give a picture: you can't pull someone out of a swamp while you're sinking in it yourself. But the sutta doesn't stop at self. The highest of the four is the one who practices for both. Then a dairy image. From a cow comes milk, from milk curd, from curd butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee, the finest of all. That cream is the person who works for self and others together. Not first one, then the other: both, in the same life, in the same day.
screen: `FOUR KINDS OF PEOPLE.` · `THE FIREBRAND: NO USE AT ALL.` · `OWN GOOD ABOVE OTHERS' GOOD ALONE.` · then, large: `THE BEST: FOR SELF AND OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Notice one thing in you that's smoking right now, a worry, an irritation, and breathe with it gently until it cools a little. Then bring to mind one person who could use a small, real help: a message, a dish washed, a question asked and listened to. Breathe in for yourself, and breathe out for them.
The firebrand. In the Numbered Sayings, the stick from a funeral pyre that's useless everywhere: the picture of a life lived for no one's good. Today's word.

664.title: Together, lives on
664.hook: an old couple, Nakula's parents, wish to meet again in future lives: shared faith, virtue, giving, wisdom
664.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers draw on the story of Nakula's parents in talks on marriage, and some Buddhist couples practice together by keeping the precepts, giving, and going to the temple as a family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the firebrand from the pyre, and your line, for self and others. Today, two people who did their practice side by side for a lifetime.

These two are not monks or nuns. They're an old married couple from the Bhagga country, known in the texts as Nakula's father and Nakula's mother, married young. One day they come to the Buddha together, and the husband says something remarkable for any marriage, ancient or modern. Since she was brought to me as a girl, he says, I don't know of ever having been unfaithful to her, not even in thought. And his wife says the same of him. Then they ask for something bigger.
screen: `AN OLD MARRIED COUPLE.` → `MARRIED YOUNG.` → `NOT EVEN IN THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: We want to see each other not only in this life, but in lives to come. Is there a way? In the Buddhist picture, life doesn't end at one death; beings are carried from life to life by what they've done and become. So the couple's question is a real one, and the Buddha takes it seriously. Yes, he says. If a husband and wife both wish to see each other in this life and the next, let them be equal in four things. Equal in faith, the trust that sets you on the path. Equal in virtue, the way you keep your conduct. Equal in generosity, the open hand. Equal in wisdom, seeing how things really are. If those four are shared, they will see each other in this life and in the life to come. Notice what's not on the list: not looks, not money, not even shared tastes in food. The bond he points to is a shared practice, two people walking the same way at the same pace, and it's a list you can work on together. Elsewhere in the Numbered Sayings, the Buddha names Nakula's father and mother as foremost among his lay followers in one quality: trust, the kind of closeness people can lean on. An honor shared by a husband and wife, and a happy marriage held up as a model.
screen: `MEET AGAIN IN LIVES TO COME.` · `SAME FAITH, SAME VIRTUE.` · `SAME GIVING, SAME WISDOM.` · then, large: `TOGETHER, LIVES ON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone close, a partner, a parent, a friend, a sibling, and picture their face. Go gently through the four: something you both trust in, a way of behaving you both care about, a way you both like to give, something you've both come to understand. Rest with whichever one you share most, and let a little gratitude for it in.
Together. Nakula's parents, the old couple of the Numbered Sayings, and the four things the Buddha said keep two lives side by side: faith, virtue, giving and wisdom, shared. Today's word.
Your line: side by side. Faith, virtue, giving and wisdom, shared, and two lives keep walking together. Day six hundred sixty-four.

665.title: Five remembrances
665.hook: I will age, sicken, die, be parted from what I love, and I am heir to my deeds
665.howItsDone: Some Buddhist monasteries and lay groups recite the five remembrances as part of morning or evening chanting, and teachers offer them as a reflection for anyone, ordained or not.

segments.voice: Yesterday: an old couple, and four things shared so they could stay side by side. Today closes a week, with five lines to say to yourself.

A list short enough to fit on a card, and meant for everyone: man or woman, householder or monk. The Buddha says these five things should be reflected on often. They're the medicine for something met four days ago, the three intoxications: the pride of being young, of being well, of being alive, which makes people careless.
screen: `SHORT ENOUGH FOR A CARD.` → `MEANT FOR EVERYONE.` → `MEDICINE FOR PRIDE.`

segments.voice: Here are the five, in plain words. One: I am of the nature to age; I haven't gone beyond aging. Two: I am of the nature to get sick; I haven't gone beyond sickness. Three: I am of the nature to die; I haven't gone beyond death. Four: everything and everyone dear to me will change, and I will be parted from them. Five: I am the owner of my deeds, heir to my deeds, born of my deeds, bound to my deeds; whatever I do, good or bad, I will inherit it. It sounds grim. But the sutta explains why each line helps. Thinking on aging wears down the pride of youth. On sickness, the pride of health. On death, the pride of being alive. On parting, the clinging to what's dear. And thinking on deeds wears down misconduct in body, speech and mind. The first four are about what you can't control; the fifth is about the one thing you can. That's the turn. You can't stop the clock or keep everyone forever, but what you do today becomes what you inherit. Heir is the key word: like an estate, your deeds are passed down to you, the good with the bad. In some monasteries and homes, these five are chanted as a daily reflection.
screen: `AGING, SICKNESS, DEATH.` · `PARTED FROM WHAT I LOVE.` · `EACH ONE WEARS DOWN A PRIDE.` · then, large: `HEIR TO MY DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, then say the lines inwardly, slowly, one every few breaths: I will grow old; I may grow ill; I will die; what I love will change, and I will part from it; I am heir to my deeds. If a line feels heavy, stay with the breath until it softens, and let the last line point somewhere: what you do is yours to shape.
Five remembrances. Aging, sickness, death, parting, and deeds: the five things the Buddha asked everyone to reflect on often, to wear down pride and steady the hand. Today's word.
Your line: heir to my deeds. Four lines name what passes, and one names what stays yours. A week of the Numbered Sayings, done.

chat.meaning: In AN 5.57, thinking on aging, sickness, death and parting wears down pride and clinging, and the fifth, heir to my deeds, wears down misconduct.
